passages.title: Reading Comprehension I – Writing systems and symbolic languages
passages.instructions: Read the following passage carefully, and answer the questions that follow. For items 1–15 choose the most appropriate alternative for each item based on the information in the text.
paragraphs: There is no human society which does not possess language, although only a small proportion of all the languages in the world have been written down. Many system have been developed by which a language can be written down and there are literally dozens of writing systems in use around the world. Some systems are alphabetical, such as the Latin alphabetical, or the Cyrillic alphabet, used for many Slav languages such as Russian. Some systems use a syllabary, where a symbol represents a single syllable, such as writing system derived from Geez, used in some Eritrean and Ethiopian languages. Other systems use a single symbol or ideograph, to convey a whole word, or concept, such as the Chinese system. Other important writing systems are those used for Arabic, and many languages in India.

As well as written languages, there is the international languages of special signs and symbols which is used everywhere to give directions or remind people of regulations. In every city in the world, we can see how useful these signs are especially as traffic symbols. In the street we see signs that tell as not to park our car, that a bus stops here, or that the speed limit is 40Kms per hour. There are signs that say “No Smoking” in a place of work, or “silence” in a library.

In addition there are special systems which have been invented for people with certain disabilities. For example, the Braille writing system is used for blind people. It consists of a series of raised dots and was invented by the French man Louis Braille in the nineteenth century. It is in use all over the world and it can now be used by blinded people with the aid of computers. A person can dictate a massage in to a computer and this is then transcribed and printed out in Braille. The only problem with Braille is that the books are very thick and heavy and consequently quite expensive.

A fourth kind of symbolic language is the sign of languages which deaf people have developed, using the hands & fingers and facial expressions. Sign language can express meanings as complex as spoken language and has been studied by linguists. Sign language is not international, because deaf people in each country have developed their own variation. For example, British Sign Language is different from American Sign Language so that deaf people from the two countries cannot understand each other, except when they write. In the future it is hoped that the system of sign language in different countries will be standardized.
passages.note: Text kept exactly as printed. Obvious typos in the original (not corrected so that line references stay valid): 'Many system' (systems), 'Latin alphabetical' (alphabet), 'there is the international languages … which is' (language), 'tell as' (us), 'blinded people' (blind), 'dictate a massage in to' (message into), 'the sign of languages' (sign languages).

passages.title: Reading Comprehension II – Environmental problems of developed and developing nations
passages.instructions: Read the following text and answer the questions that follow (items 66–80).
paragraphs: The condition of the environment is a worldwide issue. Air and water pollution do not recognize borders; poor soil conditions in one nation may reduce another countries food supply. At the same time, different regions do face different problems. One key distinction is between the environmental threats faced by developed nations, such as the united states and western European countries and developing nations such as, India and Mexico most agree that these nations many have dissimilar crises, but debate remains over whether the solutions to their problems are unique as well.

The environmental problems faced by the developed nations are largely the result of their economic strength and higher standards of living. Overconsumption is cited by many observers as a cause of resource <u>depletion</u> in the first world. Americans, and to a lesser extent western Europeans, Japanese and other residents of developed nations, are more likely to own one or more cars, purchase more food and clothes than <u>subsistence levels</u> require, and use considerable amount of electricity. Americans consume a disproportionate amount of the planet’s resources. The United States is home to five per cent of the world population but uses 25 per cent of its resources. Overall, the developed world has 23 per cent of earth’s population but consumes two thirds of the resources. Environmentalists <u>contend</u> that this high level of consumption will ultimately lead to the <u>depletion</u> of the planet’s resources resulting in <u>adverse</u> consequences for human population.

Developed nations have reduced their rate of population growth, so overpopulation is not as great as it was previously considered to be; however, because of the high level of consumption, each new person in a developed nation will use three times as much water and ten times as much energy as a child born in developing country. The industries needed to create products for consumption also affect the environment through the emission of greenhouse gases and other wastes.

In contrast, the environmental crises faced by developing nations are the result of poverty. For example, Third world countries often lack resources and sanitation facilities to provide the public with clean water. Tropical deforestation, caused by the slash-and-burn techniques of poor farmers, is another dilemma. However, as Rice University President Malcolm Gillis has observed, “agriculture is not the only manifestation of the effects of poverty on deforestation. In most, but not all, poor nations the role of poverty in deforestation is magnified by the ever-more –desperate search for fuel wood by impoverished people.” The search for wood is <u>exacerbated</u> by the key environmental problem in developing nations-overpopulation. Third world nations may consume vastly less than America and Europe but their population growth rates are much higher. These nations lack the natural resources and social services that will be needed in order to provide their <u>burgeoning</u> populations with adequate food, shelter and employment in the coming years. As developing nations move closer to first world status, the accompanying growth in industry could also affect the environment especially through the emission of greenhouse gases.
passages.note: Text kept exactly as printed, except that the six words tested in items 75–80 are marked <u>…</u>. The question says they are ‘underlined’, but the original .docx has NO underlining for them, so the marking was recovered from the passage. The passage is an abridged version of a published introduction on global environmental issues (Opposing-Viewpoints-style preface, also reproduced in S. Vijay Anand, ‘Global Environmental Issues’). The paper omits that text’s last paragraph, which discusses the 1997 Kyoto agreement and concludes: ‘If the environment truly is a worldwide issue, then the solutions may also be universal.’ Items 67 and 74, which mention Kyoto, depend on this missing paragraph. Other slips in the original: ‘another countries food supply’ (country’s), a missing full stop before ‘most agree’ and ‘many have dissimilar crises’ (may), ‘not as great as it was’ (source: ‘not as great a problem as it was’), ‘the united states’ (capitals).

questions.stem: According to the text:

options.A: Only a small number of societies do not have languages.
options.B: Many societies do not have language.
options.C: Many societies do not have a written language.
options.D: Most languages in the world have now been written down.
options.E: It is not easy to find a language which has been written down.

explanation_steps: Sentence 1: “There is no human society which does not possess language, although only a small proportion of all the languages in the world have been written down.”
‘No human society’ lacks language → A and B are false.
‘Only a small proportion … written down’ → most languages are NOT written, so D is false; but written languages still exist in dozens of systems, so E is false.
If most languages are unwritten, many societies have no written language. Answer: C.
tips: Watch for quantity words: ‘no’, ‘only a small proportion’, ‘most’, ‘many’. The correct option keeps the same quantity as the text.

similar_questions.stem: According to a text that says “Nearly every village has a school, but only a few of them have a library”, which statement is true?

options.C: Many villages have a school without a library.
options.E: Libraries are more common than schools.

explanation_steps: ‘Nearly every village has a school’ → A false; ‘only a few have a library’ → B and D false, E false.
So many villages have a school but no library. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.topic: Understanding stated details (paraphrase of a sentence)

questions.stem: What type of writing system is used by languages such as Tigrigna

options.A: The text does not give an answer
options.E: it is not really a writing system

explanation_steps: The text: “Some systems use a syllabary, where a symbol represents a single syllable, such as writing system derived from Geez, used in some Eritrean and Ethiopian languages.”
Tigrigna is an Eritrean language written in the Geez (Ge’ez) script, so the text does answer the question.
Ideographic = Chinese; Cyrillic = Russian. Answer: D (syllabary).
tips: Link the example in the question (Tigrigna) to the category word in the text (‘Eritrean … languages’).

similar_questions.stem: According to the same text, which writing system uses one symbol for a whole word or concept?
explanation_steps: “Other systems use a single symbol or ideograph, to convey a whole word, or concept, such as the Chinese system.” Answer: D.

questions.stem: What kind of writing system does Arabic use?

options.D: The text does not tell us

explanation_steps: The only sentence about Arabic: “Other important writing systems are those used for Arabic, and many languages in India.”
The text names Arabic as an important system but does not say what TYPE it is.
The instruction says answer ‘based on the information in the text’, so outside knowledge (Arabic script is alphabetic – strictly an abjad) must not be used. Answer: D.
tips: If a fact is not stated in the passage, choose ‘The text does not tell us’ – even if you know the answer from general knowledge.

similar_questions.stem: A passage says: “Many animals live in the Danakil desert, and the area is also rich in salt.” What does the passage say about the temperature of the Danakil?

options.D: The passage does not tell us.

explanation_steps: The passage mentions animals and salt only; temperature is not mentioned.
General knowledge (the Danakil is very hot) is not what the question asks. Answer: D.

textbook_ref.topic: Distinguishing stated information from outside knowledge

questions.stem: The language of signs and symbols mentioned in paragraph two:

options.E: Is not very easy to understand

explanation_steps: Paragraph 2: “there is the international languages of special signs and symbols which is used everywhere …”.

‘Used everywhere’ and ‘in every city in the world’ contradict B; examples include No Smoking and Silence, so C (‘only traffic’) is false; the text calls it a language, so D is false; nothing suggests E.
Answer: A.
tips: Words like ‘only’ in an option (C) are often traps – check whether the text gives other examples.

similar_questions.stem: According to paragraph four, sign language
explanation_steps: “Sign language is not international, because deaf people in each country have developed their own variation.” Answer: C.

questions.stem: What is the main use of the signs and symbols?

options.A: They encourage people to stop smoking
options.B: To remind people of certain rules
options.C: They are found in cities all over the world
options.E: They are useful for people who cannot read or write

explanation_steps: The text states their use directly: they are used “to give directions or remind people of regulations”.
‘Regulations’ = rules → B.
A and D are single examples, not the main use; C says where they are found, not what they are used for; E is not mentioned. Answer: B.
tips: ‘Main use/purpose’ questions: find the general statement (often with ‘to …’), not one example.

similar_questions.stem: In the same text, what is the purpose of the Braille system?

options.B: To let blind people read and write

explanation_steps: Paragraph 3: special systems were invented for people with disabilities; “the Braille writing system is used for blind people”. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Identifying purpose / general statement vs example

questions.stem: What is the disadvantage of the Braille writing system?

options.A: It cannot be used with computers
options.C: It was invented a long time ago
options.D: It takes a long time to read a massage
options.E: It is a very complicated system

explanation_steps: Paragraph 3 ends: “The only problem with Braille is that the books are very thick and heavy and consequently quite expensive.”
‘Problem’ = disadvantage → B. A is contradicted (it can be used with computers); C is a fact but not described as a problem; D and E are not mentioned. Answer: B.
tips: Synonym spotting: disadvantage = problem = drawback.

similar_questions.stem: According to the text, why are Braille books expensive?

options.B: Because they are thick and heavy
options.D: Because they were invented in France

explanation_steps: “… the books are very thick and heavy and consequently quite expensive.” ‘Consequently’ shows the cause. Answer: B.

questions.stem: In paragraph three, the word “It” in line three means:
explanation_steps: Paragraph 3: “… the Braille writing system is used for blind people. It consists of a series of raised dots … It is in use all over the world and it can now be used by blinded people with the aid of computers.”
Every ‘It’ here is the subject of statements about the writing system (raised dots, invented by Louis Braille, in use all over the world).
Answer: D (the Braille system).
tips: Pronoun reference: replace ‘It’ with each option and read the sentence – only the correct one makes sense (‘Braille is in use all over the world’).

similar_questions.stem: “Louis Braille lost his sight as a child. He later invented a system of raised dots.” The word ‘He’ refers to
explanation_steps: ‘He’ is singular, male and a person who can invent → Louis Braille. Answer: B.

questions.stem: How can blind people communicate with a computer?

options.A: They can use a system of raised dots.
options.B: They can dictate to the computers.
options.C: The computer can read a Braille message.

explanation_steps: “A person can dictate a massage [message] in to a computer and this is then transcribed and printed out in Braille.”
So the person speaks (dictates) to the computer → B. Raised dots are the output, not the way of communicating with the computer. Answer: B.
tips: Read the sentence about computers carefully: input = dictation; output = printed Braille.

similar_questions.stem: What does the computer do after a blind person dictates a message?

options.B: It transcribes it and prints it in Braille
options.D: It sends it to a deaf person

explanation_steps: “… this is then transcribed and printed out in Braille.” Answer: B.

questions.stem: In paragraph four, the phrase “the two countries” refers to:

options.A: The deaf and the people who can hear

explanation_steps: The sentence before: “British Sign Language is different from American Sign Language so that deaf people from the two countries cannot understand each other …”.
The two countries named are Britain and America (USA). Answer: B.
tips: Reference words point back to the nearest matching nouns – here ‘British’ and ‘American’.

similar_questions.stem: “Eritrea and Sudan share a long border. Trade between the two neighbours is growing.” ‘The two neighbours’ refers to
explanation_steps: The nouns just before are Eritrea and Sudan. Answer: B.

questions.stem: How deaf Americans communicate with deaf people from Britain?

options.B: The answer is not given in the text

explanation_steps: “… deaf people from the two countries cannot understand each other, except when they write.”
Their sign languages are different, so A is wrong; Braille is for the blind (E).
The only way given is writing. Answer: D.
tips: ‘except when …’ introduces the one exception – the answer is often hidden there.

similar_questions.stem: According to the passage, why can’t deaf people from Britain and the USA understand each other’s signing?

options.A: Because sign language is not complex
options.B: Because each country developed its own sign language

explanation_steps: “Sign language is not international, because deaf people in each country have developed their own variation.” Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Grammar slip in the stem: ‘How deaf Americans communicate …’ should be ‘How do deaf Americans communicate …?’. The meaning is clear and the answer is not affected.

questions.stem: How many different kinds of symbolic languages are mentioned?
explanation_steps: Count the kinds: (1) written languages / writing systems (paragraph 1); (2) the international language of signs and symbols (paragraph 2); (3) special systems for disabled people – Braille (paragraph 3); (4) sign languages of deaf people (paragraph 4).
The text itself confirms it: “A fourth kind of symbolic language is …”. Answer: A.
tips: Each paragraph of this text introduces one kind; the word ‘fourth’ in the last paragraph is the clue.

similar_questions.stem: Which kind of symbolic language does the passage describe in paragraph three?

options.C: Systems for people with disabilities, such as Braille

explanation_steps: Paragraph 3: “special systems which have been invented for people with certain disabilities … the Braille writing system”. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.topic: Text organisation – one idea per paragraph

questions.stem: A good title for paragraph four would be :
explanation_steps: Paragraph 4 is about sign languages: how they work, that they are not international, and that they may be standardized.
B is contradicted (‘not international’); E is only one example; C is too broad (the paragraph is about their language, not deaf people in general); A – invention is not discussed.
Answer: D.
tips: A title must cover the WHOLE paragraph – not too narrow (one example) and not too broad.

similar_questions.stem: A good title for paragraph three of the same passage would be

options.C: Braille: a writing system for the blind

explanation_steps: Paragraph 3 describes Braille – what it is, its inventor, its use with computers and its problem.
A, B and D are details only. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The word “possess” in the first paragraph has closest meaning with:
explanation_steps: “There is no human society which does not possess language” – every society HAS language.
possess = have / own. Answer: C.
tips: Substitute each option into the sentence: ‘no society which does not have language’ keeps the meaning.

similar_questions.stem: “Few families in the village possess a car.” The word ‘possess’ means
explanation_steps: possess = own/have. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The word “convey” in the first paragraph has closest meaning with:
explanation_steps: “Other systems use a single symbol or ideograph, to convey a whole word, or concept” – the symbol EXPRESSES (communicates) a word.
convey = express, communicate, carry (a meaning). Answer: A.
tips: Do not confuse convey (carry/express) with convince (make someone believe).

similar_questions.stem: “Her face conveyed deep sadness.” The word ‘conveyed’ means
explanation_steps: Her face showed/expressed sadness. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The  word “standardized” in the last paragraph has closest meaning with:
explanation_steps: “In the future it is hoped that the system of sign language in different countries will be standardized.”
At present each country has its own variation; standardized = made the same / uniform everywhere.
Of the options, ‘be identical’ (the same) is closest. A and C are opposites. Answer: B.
tips: Use the contrast in the paragraph: now = different in each country → future hope = the same.

similar_questions.stem: “All the schools use a standardized exam.” This means the exam is
explanation_steps: Standardized = made the same according to one standard. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Haben (16) _____ the bus and walked quickly towards his house.
explanation_steps: The story is in the past: ‘… and walked quickly towards his house.’
Two completed actions in sequence joined by ‘and’ take the same tense → past simple: got off … walked.
A/D are present perfect (and A has no ‘off’), C is present, E (past continuous) is for an action in progress, not a completed step in a sequence. Answer: B.
tips: Parallel verbs joined by ‘and’ normally share the same tense (got off … and walked).

similar_questions.stem: Selam ____ the taxi and paid the driver.
explanation_steps: ‘paid’ is past simple; the parallel action is also past simple. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: A sequence of completed past events in a story is told in the past simple.

questions.stem: It was a long day at work, and all he (17) ____ to do at that moment was to put his feet up …
explanation_steps: The clause refers to ‘that moment’ in the past and the main verb is ‘was’.
Past simple ‘wanted’ is needed. ‘Want’ is a stative verb, so the continuous (E) is not used; B is not a finite verb. Answer: C.
tips: Stative verbs (want, know, like, need) are not normally used in continuous tenses.

similar_questions.stem: When I got home, all I ____ was a cup of tea.
explanation_steps: Past context (got home) + stative verb → past simple ‘wanted’. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Stative verbs such as ‘want’ are used in simple, not continuous, forms.

questions.stem: … all he wanted to do at that moment was to put his feet up and (18) ___ television for a while.
explanation_steps: The blank is parallel to ‘to put his feet up’: ‘to put … and (to) watch’.
After ‘and’ in a series of infinitives, the second ‘to’ is usually dropped → bare infinitive ‘watch’. Answer: C.
tips: Parallel structure: to put … and watch (not ‘and watching/watched’).

similar_questions.stem: She decided to finish her homework and ____ to bed early.
explanation_steps: Parallel with ‘to finish’ → (to) go. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: Infinitives joined by ‘and’ share one ‘to’: to put … and watch.

questions.stem: But something is wrong and it (19) _____ him only a moment to realize what it was.
explanation_steps: The narrative is in the past (‘It was a long day’, ‘His television set was not there!’).
‘It took him only a moment to realize’ = a completed past event → past simple ‘took’.
The paper’s ‘something is wrong’ is a slip for ‘something was wrong’; it does not change the answer. Answer: E.
tips: Pattern: It + take + person + time + to-infinitive: ‘It took me an hour to finish.’

similar_questions.stem: It ____ us three hours to reach Keren yesterday.
explanation_steps: ‘yesterday’ → past simple ‘took’. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: A sequence of completed past events in a story is told in the past simple.

questions.review_flag: Tense slip in the passage: ‘But something is wrong’ should read ‘But something was wrong’. The answer (took) is unaffected.

questions.stem: … it took him only a moment to realize what it (20) ______. His television set was not there!
explanation_steps: ‘what it ___’ is a noun clause after a past verb (realized) → past tense.
Subject ‘it’ is singular → ‘was’. Answer: B.
tips: Sequence of tenses: after a past reporting/thinking verb, the noun clause moves into the past.

similar_questions.stem: She suddenly understood what the problem ____.
explanation_steps: Past main verb + singular subject → was. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.topic: Sequence of tenses in noun clauses

questions.stem: Somebody (20) ___ in the house through the window, … [item 21 – printed as the second blank (20)]
explanation_steps: The story is in the past; the break-in is a single completed action.
Strictly, because it happened before ‘he understood what had happened’, the past perfect ‘had sneaked’ would be best – but it is not offered.
Of the options, only the past simple ‘sneaked’ fits a completed past action (D, past continuous, would describe an action in progress). Answer: B.
tips: When the ideal past perfect is missing, choose the simple past for a completed earlier action.

similar_questions.stem: When we arrived, the film ____ already ____.
explanation_steps: Action completed before another past action (arrived) → past perfect ‘had started’. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: The earlier of two past actions is ideally in the past perfect; the past simple is acceptable when the order is clear.

questions.review_flag: Blank numbering in the paper is off by one from here on (duplicate ‘(20)’): item 21 is the blank printed as (20 – second occurrence). Also, the ideal form ‘had sneaked’ is not among the options; B (sneaked) is the best available.

questions.stem: … through the window, which he had left it open to (21) ____ ventilated. [item 22 – printed as blank (21)]
explanation_steps: The house was to receive air: a passive infinitive of purpose → ‘to be ventilated’.
‘to’ must be followed by a base form: be/have/become. ‘to have ventilated’ and ‘to become ventilated’ do not express the intended passive meaning idiomatically.
Answer: C. (Note: the paper’s ‘which he had left it open’ has an extra ‘it’; correct: ‘which he had left open’.)
tips: Passive infinitive = to be + past participle (to be ventilated, to be cleaned).

similar_questions.stem: The documents need to ____ signed by the director.
explanation_steps: Passive infinitive after ‘need to’: to be signed. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: to be + past participle

questions.review_flag: Blank numbering in the paper is off by one from here on (duplicate ‘(20)’): item 22 is the blank printed as (21). The passage also has an extra pronoun: ‘which he had left it open’ should be ‘which he had left open’.

questions.stem: Logically, how can he leave a window unclosed even though he (22) ___ the area which is crowded with urchins and thieves? [item 23 – printed as blank (22)]
explanation_steps: This sentence is the narrator’s comment in the present (‘how can he leave …?’, ‘the area which is crowded’).
A present general fact about Haben → present simple ‘knows’ (know is stative).
If the question were in the past (‘how could he leave …’), ‘knew’ would fit; with ‘can’ and ‘is crowded’, D matches best. E is passive and wrong in meaning. Answer: D.
tips: Match the tense of the clause to the other verbs in the same sentence (can … is crowded → knows).

similar_questions.stem: How can she forget her keys again when she ____ we are leaving early?
explanation_steps: Present context (how can she forget) + stative verb → knows. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Present simple for facts / tense consistency

questions.review_flag: Blank numbering in the paper is off by one from here on (duplicate ‘(20)’): item 23 is the blank printed as (22). The passage switches between past narrative and present comment, so A (knew) could be argued; D matches the present ‘how can he leave … which is crowded’ in the same sentence.

questions.stem: When he asked the police for help, they replied, “we (23) _____ there by tomorrow morning.” [item 24 – printed as blank (23)]
explanation_steps: ‘will there’ (A) and ‘ought to there’ (D) lack a verb; ‘had better there’ (E) likewise – ungrammatical.
‘by tomorrow morning’ (by + future time) is the classic signal for the future perfect: ‘We will have been there by tomorrow morning’ (= our visit will be completed by then).
C (‘should be there’) is grammatical too, but it is a modal of expectation, not a tense; the instruction asks for the most appropriate TENSE. Answer: B.
tips: ‘by + future time’ (by tomorrow, by next week) → future perfect: will have + past participle.

similar_questions.stem: By the end of this year, my father ____ at Sawa for ten years.
explanation_steps: ‘By the end of this year’ (by + future time) + a duration up to that future point (for ten years) → future perfect.
‘will work’ cannot express a period completed by a future time; C, D and E do not refer to the future. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: will have + past participle for an action completed before a future time (by …).

questions.review_flag: Blank numbering in the paper is off by one from here on (duplicate ‘(20)’): item 24 is the blank printed as (23). C (‘should be there’) is also grammatical; B is keyed because the item tests tenses and ‘by tomorrow morning’ signals the future perfect.

questions.stem: “If Haben (24) ____ about the cause of the theft tomorrow, he will find no one to blame …” [item 25 – printed as blank (24)]
explanation_steps: Main clause: ‘he will find’ → first conditional: If + present simple, … will + base verb.
Haben receives the action (someone questions him) → present simple passive: ‘is questioned’.
B puts ‘will’ in the if-clause (wrong); C and E belong to other conditional types; A has the wrong subject agreement. Answer: D.
tips: Never use ‘will’ in the if-clause of a first conditional: If he is asked … he will answer.

similar_questions.stem: If the parcel ____ today, you will receive it on Friday.
explanation_steps: First conditional (will receive) + passive meaning → is sent. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: If + present simple, will + base form.

questions.review_flag: Blank numbering in the paper is off by one from here on (duplicate ‘(20)’): item 25 is the blank printed as (24).

questions.stem: Number (26) ___ hundred and two, the house next door to us, is for sale.
explanation_steps: Numbers like 100 are said ‘a hundred’ or ‘one hundred’: ‘a hundred and two’ = 102.
‘one’ is not offered; ‘hundred’ begins with a consonant sound /h/, so ‘a’, not ‘an’. Answer: A.
tips: a hundred, a thousand, a million = one hundred / one thousand / one million.

similar_questions.stem: The school has about ____ thousand students.
explanation_steps: ‘a thousand’ = one thousand; /θ/ is a consonant sound. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘a’ is used with hundred/thousand/million meaning ‘one’.

questions.stem: Number a hundred and two, (27) ___ house next door to us, is for sale.
explanation_steps: ‘house next door to us’ is one particular, identified house (there is only one house next door) → ‘the’.
It is in apposition to ‘Number 102’, identifying it. Answer: A.
tips: Use ‘the’ when the noun is made specific by a phrase after it (the house next door, the man in the red shirt).

similar_questions.stem: Mr Tesfay, ____ teacher who lives opposite us, is retiring.
explanation_steps: The phrase ‘who lives opposite us’ identifies one specific teacher → the. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘the’ for a noun identified by what follows it.

questions.stem: It’s quite (28) ____ nice house with … big rooms.
explanation_steps: Singular countable noun described for the first time (one of many nice houses) → indefinite article.
Word order with ‘quite’: quite + a + adjective + noun (‘quite a nice house’). ‘nice’ begins with a consonant sound → ‘a’. Answer: C.
tips: quite a …, such a …, what a … : the article comes after quite/such/what.

similar_questions.stem: It was quite ____ interesting lecture.
explanation_steps: quite + a/an + adj + noun; ‘interesting’ starts with a vowel sound → an. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: quite + a/an + adjective + singular noun.

questions.stem: It’s quite a nice house with (29) ____ big rooms.
explanation_steps: ‘rooms’ is a plural countable noun used in a general, non-specific sense.
Plural nouns take no indefinite article (a/an only with singular). ‘the’ would need the rooms to be identified; ‘any’ is used in questions/negatives. Answer: E (zero article).
tips: a/an never goes with plural nouns: a room → rooms (no article).

similar_questions.stem: Our school has ____ modern laboratories.
explanation_steps: Plural, general meaning → zero article. Answer: D.

textbook_ref.rule: Zero article with plural countable nouns in a general sense.

questions.stem: (30) ____ back windows look out on to a park.
explanation_steps: ‘back windows’ means the back windows of THIS house – already known from the context.
Specific plural noun → ‘the’. Answer: B.
tips: Parts of something already mentioned take ‘the’: a house … the roof, the door, the back windows.

similar_questions.stem: We bought a new car, but ____ tyres were already worn.
explanation_steps: The tyres of the car just mentioned → specific → the. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘the’ for parts of something already mentioned.

questions.stem: The back windows look out on to (31) ___ park.
explanation_steps: ‘park’ is mentioned for the first time and has not been identified → indefinite article.
Singular countable, consonant sound → ‘a park’. Answer: B.
tips: First mention of a singular countable noun → a/an; later mentions → the.

similar_questions.stem: Yesterday I saw ____ old man selling fruit near the market.
explanation_steps: First mention, singular, vowel sound (old) → an. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: a/an for the first mention of a singular countable noun.

questions.stem: This stream form a ______ between my land and his.
explanation_steps: A line that separates two pieces of land is a boundary.
tributary = a stream flowing into a bigger river; territory = an area of land; contributory/exemplary are adjectives. Answer: A.
tips: Collocation: ‘form a boundary between A and B’.

similar_questions.stem: The Mereb River forms part of the ____ between Eritrea and Ethiopia.
explanation_steps: A river separating two countries forms a boundary. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Word choice – land and water vocabulary

questions.review_flag: Subject–verb agreement slip in the stem: ‘This stream form’ should be ‘This stream forms’. The answer is unaffected.

questions.stem: Some rich people in the past gave money to run ____ schools to which poor children could go without paying.
explanation_steps: Schools run with money given by rich people so that poor children pay nothing are ‘charity schools’ (charity = giving help/money to people in need).
Mission/church schools are run by religious organisations; government schools by the state – the stem stresses private donations. Answer: B.
tips: ‘charity’ as a noun modifier: charity school, charity shop, charity organisation.

similar_questions.stem: She donated all the money from the concert to ____ for orphans.
explanation_steps: Giving money to help people in need → charity. Answer: A.

questions.stem: There is the man in the river fully clothed who is ______.
explanation_steps: ‘to be in difficulties’ (or ‘in difficulty’) is the fixed phrase for a swimmer or boat in danger / in trouble in the water.
‘in problems’ and ‘in hazards’ are not English idioms; ‘in hardship’ refers to long-term poverty or suffering. Answer: C.
tips: Fixed expressions: be in difficulties, be in trouble, be in danger.

similar_questions.stem: The fishing boat was ____ in the storm, so the coast guard went to help.
explanation_steps: A boat in danger at sea is ‘in difficulties’. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Romeo and Juliet _____ written by William Shakespeare.
explanation_steps: ‘Romeo and Juliet’ here is the TITLE of one play, so it is singular.
Passive past: was + written. Answer: D.
tips: Titles of books, plays and films are singular even if they contain ‘and’ or a plural: ‘Great Expectations is …’.

similar_questions.stem: ‘Things Fall Apart’ ____ written by Chinua Achebe.
explanation_steps: Book title → singular → was written. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: A title is a single thing and takes a singular verb.

questions.stem: Students must study hard ______ they should fail.
explanation_steps: ‘lest’ = ‘so that … not / for fear that’, and it is typically followed by ‘should’: study hard lest they should fail = so that they will not fail.
‘so that they should fail’ gives the opposite meaning; ‘so as to’ needs an infinitive. Answer: C.
tips: lest + subject + (should) + base verb = in order that … not.

similar_questions.stem: Walk carefully ____ you should slip on the wet floor.
explanation_steps: Purpose of avoiding something + ‘should’ → lest. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: lest + (should) + base form = so that … not.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?

options.A: I asked him how old he was?
options.B: I asked him how old he was.
options.C: I asked him, “How old was he.”
options.D: I asked him, “How old he was?”
options.E: I asked him, how old he was.

explanation_steps: An indirect (reported) question is a statement: normal word order (he was) and a full stop, no question mark, no comma, no quotation marks.
A has a question mark; C and D use quotation marks with wrong word order/punctuation (direct form would be: I asked him, “How old are you?”); E has an unnecessary comma. Answer: B.
tips: Reported questions end with a full stop and use statement word order.

similar_questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?

options.A: She wanted to know where I lived?
options.B: She wanted to know where I lived.
options.C: She wanted to know, where I lived.
options.D: She wanted to know “where I lived.”
options.E: She wanted to know where did I live?

explanation_steps: Indirect question → statement order and full stop. Answer: B.

questions.stem: _____ the heavy rain, we enjoyed playing football.

options.C: In spite of the fact that

explanation_steps: The blank is followed by a noun phrase (‘the heavy rain’), not a clause.
In spite of / despite + noun phrase. ‘Although’, ‘in spite of the fact that’ and ‘despite the fact that’ need a clause (subject + verb). ‘Despite of’ is never correct. Answer: B.
tips: Although + clause; in spite of / despite + noun (no ‘of’ after despite).

similar_questions.stem: ____ his illness, he came to school.

options.E: In spite of the fact that

explanation_steps: Noun phrase (his illness) → despite. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Contrast linkers – although / in spite of / despite

questions.stem: I am late because my alarm clock never ____ this morning.
explanation_steps: An alarm clock that rings ‘goes off’ (phrasal verb go off = ring/sound suddenly).
came on / turned on are used for lights and machines being switched on; ‘ring out’ is the wrong form (it should be past tense) and not the usual collocation. Answer: C.
tips: go off = (alarm/bomb) ring or explode; (food) become bad; (lights) stop working.

similar_questions.stem: Everyone left the building when the fire alarm ____.
explanation_steps: An alarm sounding → went off. Answer: A.

questions.stem: When Franklin Roosevelt decided to run for a fourth term the opposition said that he was _____.
explanation_steps: The meaning is ‘more than is acceptable for the job’ → too + adjective.
‘so old’ needs a result clause (so old that …); ‘oldest’ needs ‘the’ and a comparison; ‘very older’ is ungrammatical. Answer: B.
tips: too + adjective = more than is acceptable (often with a negative result).

similar_questions.stem: This box is ____ heavy for a child to carry.
explanation_steps: too + adjective + for … to = excessively. Answer: B.

questions.stem: If I had given you five thousand Nakfa _____?

options.A: what would you do with it
options.B: what will you have done with it
options.C: what will you do with it
options.D: what would you have done with it

explanation_steps: If-clause: past perfect (had given) → third conditional (unreal past).
Main clause: would have + past participle → ‘what would you have done with it?’. Answer: D.
tips: Third conditional: If + had + V3, … would have + V3.

similar_questions.stem: If you had studied harder, you ____ the exam.
explanation_steps: had studied → would have passed. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

questions.stem: You ___ do what I say or else you will get into trouble.
explanation_steps: ‘or else you will get into trouble’ is a warning of a bad result → ‘had better’ (strong advice with a warning).
‘had better … or (else) …’ is the typical pattern. ‘must’ is also grammatical, which is why this item is not fully certain; C, D and E do not fit the meaning. Answer: B.
tips: had better + base verb (no ‘to’) – often followed by ‘or (else)’ + a threat.

similar_questions.stem: You ____ take an umbrella, or you’ll get wet.
explanation_steps: Advice with a warning (or you’ll get wet) → had better. Answer: A.

questions.review_flag: Two grammatical options: ‘had better’ (B, keyed – the standard pattern with ‘or else’ + threat) and ‘must’ (A). Check the teacher’s intended key.

questions.stem: A university that is detached from its community will gain ___ social support.
explanation_steps: ‘support’ is uncountable → little / a little (few, a few and many are for countable plurals).
The meaning is negative (being detached is bad → almost no support) → ‘little’. ‘a little’ is positive (some). Answer: B.
tips: little/few = almost none (negative); a little/a few = some (positive).

similar_questions.stem: He was so busy that he had ____ time to eat.
explanation_steps: time is uncountable; negative meaning (so busy) → little. Answer: C.

questions.stem: He made her ___ him the answer.
explanation_steps: Causative ‘make’ (active): make + object + bare infinitive.
‘He made her tell him the answer.’ (In the passive the ‘to’ returns: She was made to tell him.) Answer: B.
tips: make/let/have + object + base verb; get + object + to-infinitive.

similar_questions.stem: The teacher let us ____ early.
explanation_steps: let + object + bare infinitive. Answer: B.

questions.stem: No one knows what they have to do, ______?
explanation_steps: ‘No one’ makes the sentence NEGATIVE, so the tag is positive.
With no one / nobody / everyone the tag pronoun is ‘they’; the main verb is present simple (knows) → auxiliary ‘do’.
Tag: ‘do they?’ Answer: C.
tips: Negative words (no one, nothing, never, hardly) make a positive tag: Nobody came, did they?

similar_questions.stem: Nobody called while I was out, ____?
explanation_steps: Nobody = negative, past simple → positive tag ‘did they?’. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Question tags with negative words (no one, nobody)

questions.review_flag: Options D and E are identical in the original (‘did they’ printed twice). This does not affect the key (C).

questions.stem: Let’s discuss the issue, ____?
explanation_steps: ‘Let’s’ (= let us) is a suggestion that includes the speaker.
The fixed tag after ‘Let’s …’ is ‘shall we?’. (‘Let me/him …’ or an order take ‘will you?’.) Answer: B.
tips: Let’s … , shall we?   Open the door, will you?

similar_questions.stem: Let’s go to the cinema tonight, ____?
explanation_steps: Let’s → shall we. Answer: B.

questions.stem: “What are you having to start with?” I asked my wife. “I don’t know,” she said. “I’m not very hungry.” “______,” I answered.
explanation_steps: The wife’s negative sentence uses ‘am’: ‘I’m not very hungry.’
To agree with a negative statement: Neither/Nor + auxiliary + subject → ‘Nor am I.’ (or ‘I’m not either’).
D uses the wrong auxiliary (did), E has the wrong word order, B and C are ungrammatical. Answer: A.
tips: Nor/Neither + same auxiliary + subject: I’m not … → Nor am I. I can’t … → Neither can I.

similar_questions.stem: “I can’t swim.” “____.”
explanation_steps: Negative with ‘can’ → Neither can I. Answer: A.

questions.review_flag: Quotation marks in the original stem are garbled (”What are you having to start with? ‘I asked my wife, ‘I don’t know,” …); the stem is shown with corrected punctuation. The answer (Nor am I) is unaffected.

questions.stem: Halima never goes to parties. ____.
explanation_steps: ‘never’ makes the first sentence negative.
Negative additions: ‘Nor does Niema.’, ‘Neither does Niema.’ and ‘Niema doesn’t, either.’ are ALL correct (A, B, C).
A contrasting addition ‘… but Niema does’ (D) is also grammatical.
Since A, B and C (and D) are all possible, the only single choice that fits the question is E. Answer: E.
tips: When several options are equally correct and an ‘all are possible/all of the above’ option exists, choose it.

similar_questions.stem: My brother doesn’t eat meat. ____.
explanation_steps: A, B and C are all correct negative additions; E is for positive statements. Answer: D.

questions.review_flag: A, B and C are all correct (and D is a grammatical contrast), so the only defensible single key is E (‘all are possible answers’). Check the teacher’s intended key.

questions.stem: You have never read war and peace.
explanation_steps: Agreeing with a negative statement: the reply is also negative → ‘No, I haven’t.’
The auxiliary must match the statement (have → haven’t), so ‘didn’t’ (B, D) is wrong; ‘Yes’ cannot go with a negative short answer (A). Answer: C.
tips: Short answers repeat the auxiliary of the statement; to agree with a negative, say ‘No, … not’.

similar_questions.stem: You haven’t seen my keys. (agree)
explanation_steps: Negative statement + agreement → No, I haven’t. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Minor typos in the original: the book title ‘War and Peace’ is not capitalised and option D lacks its full stop after the letter (‘D Yes’).

questions.stem: Sawa is comfortable place.
explanation_steps: Agreeing with a positive statement: positive reply with the same auxiliary → ‘Yes, it is.’
‘Yes’ + positive or ‘No’ + negative only; A and B mix them; D disagrees. Answer: C.
tips: Agree with positive → Yes, … is/does/can. Disagree → No, … isn’t/doesn’t/can’t.

similar_questions.stem: Asmara is a clean city. (agree)
explanation_steps: Positive statement + agreement → Yes, it is. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Article missing in the stem: ‘Sawa is comfortable place’ should be ‘Sawa is a comfortable place’. The answer is unaffected.

questions.stem: First and foremost (51) ____ the blessing of civilization are order and safety.
explanation_steps: ‘first/foremost AMONG + a group’ = the most important in that group; the widely reproduced source text reads ‘First and foremost among the blessings of civilization …’.
‘first and foremost of the blessings’ (E) is also acceptable English (first + of + group), so both B and E are accepted.
with, between and into do not fit. Keyed answer: B (among); E (of) also accepted. (‘blessing’ should be plural ‘blessings’.)
tips: ‘foremost among’, ‘first among equals’ – among + a group of three or more; ‘the first of’ is also possible.

similar_questions.stem: Foremost ____ the causes of the accident was the poor condition of the road.
explanation_steps: foremost among + group (several causes). Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Prepositions – dependent prepositions and phrasal verbs
textbook_ref.rule: foremost among / first of + group

questions.review_flag: Two defensible options: ‘among’ (B – the wording of the published source passage) and ‘of’ (E – ‘first … of the blessings’). Both are accepted; the paper’s intended key is unknown. ‘blessing’ should be ‘blessings’.

questions.stem: If today I have a quarrel (52) ___ another man, I don’t get beaten merely because I’m physically weaker …
explanation_steps: Collocation: have a quarrel WITH somebody (about something). Answer: E.
tips: quarrel/argue/fight with someone; about something.

similar_questions.stem: He had an argument ____ his neighbour about the fence.
explanation_steps: argument with a person. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Prepositions – dependent prepositions and phrasal verbs
textbook_ref.rule: quarrel with someone

questions.stem: … because I’m physically weaker and he can knock me (53) ___.
explanation_steps: knock somebody down = hit someone so that they fall to the ground.
‘knock up’ and ‘knock off’ have other meanings (knock off = stop work); ‘knock of’ is not a phrasal verb. Answer: A.
tips: knock down (a person / a building), knock out (make unconscious).

similar_questions.stem: The old building was knocked ____ to make room for a new hospital.
explanation_steps: knock down = demolish. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Prepositions – dependent prepositions and phrasal verbs
textbook_ref.rule: knock someone down

questions.stem: I go to law, and the law will decide as fairly as it can be (54) ____ the two of us.
explanation_steps: The law decides between two people → ‘between’ (two parties). ‘among’ is used for three or more.
Answer: C. (The printed ‘can be’ is a slip for ‘can’: ‘as fairly as it can between the two of us’.)
tips: between = two people/things; among = more than two.

similar_questions.stem: The prize was shared ____ the two winners.
explanation_steps: Two winners → between. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Prepositions – dependent prepositions and phrasal verbs
textbook_ref.rule: between (two) vs among (more than two)

questions.review_flag: Slip in the passage: ‘as fairly as it can be (54) the two of us’ – ‘be’ should be deleted (‘as fairly as it can between the two of us’). The answer (between) is unaffected.

questions.stem: Moreover, the law protects me (55) ____ robbery and violence.
explanation_steps: Collocation: protect somebody FROM (or against) danger. Answer: D.
tips: protect/save/prevent … from.

similar_questions.stem: Sunglasses protect your eyes ____ strong sunlight.
explanation_steps: protect from. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Prepositions – dependent prepositions and phrasal verbs
textbook_ref.rule: protect someone from something

questions.stem: Nobody may come and break (56) ____ my house, steal my goods …
explanation_steps: break into a building = enter it illegally by force (burglary). Answer: C.
tips: break into (a house), break out (escape / start suddenly), break down (stop working).

similar_questions.stem: Thieves broke ____ the shop last night and stole the radios.
explanation_steps: Entering illegally → broke into. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Prepositions – dependent prepositions and phrasal verbs
textbook_ref.rule: break into a building

questions.stem: Nobody may come and break into my house, steal my goods or run (57) ____ my children.
explanation_steps: run off with somebody/something = take them away / steal them and escape. Answer: A.
‘run away with’ (E) is close, but ‘run off with’ is the standard phrase for stealing/kidnapping and the wording of the source text; ‘run out of’ = have none left; ‘run after’ = chase.
tips: run off with = steal and escape; run out of = finish a supply.

similar_questions.stem: The cashier ran ____ all the money from the safe.
explanation_steps: Steal and escape → ran off with. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Prepositions – dependent prepositions and phrasal verbs
textbook_ref.rule: run off with = steal / take away

questions.review_flag: Option E ‘away with’ (run away with) is close in meaning; A ‘off with’ is keyed because it is the standard phrase and the wording of the published source passage.

questions.stem: Any way, it is difficult (58) _____ us to realize how much this safety means.
explanation_steps: Pattern: It is + adjective + FOR + person + to-infinitive (It is difficult for us to realize …). Answer: B.
tips: It is easy/hard/difficult/important for someone to do something.

similar_questions.stem: It is important ____ students to revise every day.
explanation_steps: It is + adj + for + person + to … Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Prepositions – dependent prepositions and phrasal verbs
textbook_ref.rule: It is + adjective + for + person + to-infinitive

questions.stem: When my mother died I couldn’t help crying: This means

options.D: I didn’t help anybody to cry

explanation_steps: can’t/couldn’t help + -ing = cannot stop oneself from doing something.
So: I could not stop (myself) crying. Answer: C.
tips: ‘I can’t help laughing’ = I can’t stop myself laughing (nothing to do with helping people).

similar_questions.stem: “She couldn’t help laughing at the joke.” This means

options.B: She could not stop herself from laughing.

explanation_steps: couldn’t help + -ing = couldn’t stop herself. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Nothing short of death sentence will satisfy the dead man’s wife.

options.A: Death sentence will not satisfy the woman.
options.B: Anything will satisfy the woman except a death sentence.
options.C: Only a death sentence will satisfy the woman.
options.D: The woman likes to make longer sentence rather than shorter once when she writes about death.
options.E: She hardly satisfied with short of death sentence

explanation_steps: ‘nothing short of X’ = nothing less than X; only X is enough.
So only a death sentence (for the killer) will satisfy her. Answer: C.
tips: nothing short of = nothing less than = only.

similar_questions.stem: “Nothing short of a miracle can save the team now.” This means

options.A: A miracle cannot save the team.
options.B: Only a miracle can save the team.
options.C: The team does not need a miracle.

explanation_steps: nothing short of = only. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The philosopher have only interpreted the world, in various ways; the point, however, is to change it.

options.A: Changing the world is more important than interpreting it.
options.B: Philosophers have arrived at a similar conclusions regarding the interpretation of the world.
options.C: Changing the interpretation in various ways is more important than any other thing.
options.D: The most important points is changing the interpretation of the philosopher.
options.E: Interpretation is more important than changing the world.

explanation_steps: This is Karl Marx’s famous thesis: “The philosophers have only interpreted the world, in various ways; the point, however, is to change it.”
‘only interpreted … the point, however, is to change it’ → changing the world matters more than interpreting it. ‘it’ = the world, not the interpretation (C, D). Answer: A.
tips: ‘only … however’ sets up a contrast: the second idea is the important one.

similar_questions.stem: “Many people talk about the problem; the point, however, is to solve it.” This means

options.A: Talking is more important than solving.
options.B: Solving the problem is more important than talking about it.
options.E: Solving and talking are equally useless.

explanation_steps: The contrast with ‘however’ shows solving is what matters. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Agreement slip in the stem: ‘The philosopher have’ should be ‘The philosophers have’ (Marx, Theses on Feuerbach). The answer is unaffected.

questions.stem: They say,” What a beautiful garden!”

options.A: They said that what a beautiful garden.
options.B: They exclaimed what a beautiful garden.
options.C: They exclaimed how beautiful that garden is.
options.D: They exclaimed how beautiful the garden was.
options.E: They exclaim how was a beautiful garden.

explanation_steps: Exclamations are reported with ‘exclaim(ed)’ + how/what + statement word order: exclaimed how beautiful the garden was / what a beautiful garden it was.
A and B keep the exclamation form without subject + verb; C mixes past ‘exclaimed’ with present ‘is’ and ‘that’; E has question word order.

Strictly, the reporting verb in the paper is present (‘They say’), so the ideal answer would be ‘They exclaim how beautiful the garden is’ – not offered. D is the only correctly formed report. Answer: D.
tips: Reporting exclamations: What a …! / How …! → exclaimed that it was a very … / exclaimed how … it was.

similar_questions.stem: He said, “How clever the girl is!”

options.A: He exclaimed how clever the girl is.
options.B: He exclaimed that the girl was very clever.
options.C: He said how clever is the girl.
options.D: He exclaimed what clever the girl was.
options.E: He asked how clever the girl was.

questions.stem:
PART II: PARAGRAPH WRITING. Write a meaningful and grammatically correct paragraph of about 200 words by choosing ONE of the two topics provided. You are advised to spend ONE HOUR writing your paragraph. During this time, you should plan, and make any necessary changes to your paragraph. Your paragraph will be graded on content, language and organization.
Topics:
1. The negative effect of peer pressure
2. Compare Asmara to Addis-Ababa using the information given in the table below.

stem_tables.title: Topic 2 – Asmara and Addis Ababa (as printed in the paper)
rows: Diversity of ethnic groups, welcoming people
More people living on the streets, stealing
Semenawi Bahri national park and the Red sea
Diversified wild life, Hawasa national park
stem_tables.note: Recovered from the .docx table. Typos kept as printed: ‘2.355m’ = 2,355 m; ‘Luck of housing’ = lack of housing.

questions.answer:
Write ONE paragraph on ONE topic. Model paragraph for Topic 1 (200 words):
Peer pressure can have serious negative effects on young people. Peer pressure is the influence that friends and classmates of the same age have on the way a person thinks and behaves. First of all, it can push teenagers into harmful habits. A student who wants to be accepted by a group may start smoking or drinking alcohol simply because his friends do it, even though he knows these habits damage his health. Secondly, peer pressure often harms academic performance. When friends prefer to skip classes, play cards or chat on their phones all night, a student may follow them instead of studying, and his results begin to fall. In addition, peer pressure can destroy a young person’s self-confidence and identity. Teenagers who always try to dress, speak and act like others gradually forget their own values and feel worthless when they cannot keep up. Finally, it can create conflict at home, because children may lie to their parents or disobey them in order to please their friends. In conclusion, although friends are important, young people should choose their friends carefully and learn to say “no”, so that peer pressure does not ruin their health, their education and their future.

Model paragraph for Topic 2 (223 words):
Asmara, the capital of Eritrea, and Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia, are similar in some ways but different in many others. To begin with, both cities are located in the highlands. Asmara stands at 2,300 metres above sea level, while Addis Ababa is slightly higher at 2,355 metres. As a result, both cities enjoy a moderate climate, although Addis Ababa is mostly rainy. However, the two capitals differ greatly in size and age. Addis Ababa has a population of about 3,000,000, six times larger than Asmara’s 500,000, and according to the table it was founded about 800 years ago, whereas Asmara is only about 400 years old. Their languages are also different: people in Asmara mainly use Tigrigna and Arabic, but in Addis Ababa Amharic is the main language. Each city has its own strengths and weaknesses. Asmara is famous for its peace and security, but it suffers from a lack of housing. On the other hand, Addis Ababa has a great diversity of ethnic groups and welcoming people, yet more people live on the streets and stealing is a problem. Finally, both cities attract tourists: Asmara offers Semenawi Bahri national park and the Red Sea, while Addis Ababa offers diverse wildlife and Hawasa national park. In short, Asmara is smaller and safer, while Addis Ababa is bigger, older and more diverse.

explanation_steps: Choose the topic you have more ideas and vocabulary for. Topic 1 is an argument or explanation paragraph (effects). Topic 2 is a comparison/contrast paragraph and must use the table.
Spend about 10 minutes planning with the template: write the topic sentence, 3–4 supporting points with an example or explanation each, and a concluding sentence.

Topic sentence: state the main idea and the controlling idea, e.g. ‘Peer pressure can have serious negative effects on young people.’ or ‘Asmara and Addis Ababa are similar in some ways but different in many others.’
Supporting sentences: introduce each point with a linker (first of all, secondly, in addition, finally). Support it with an example or result (Topic 1) or with figures from the table (Topic 2).

Topic 2: do not just copy the table row by row. Compare with whereas / while / but / on the other hand / both … / six times larger than / slightly higher than. Correct the table’s typos in your writing (2,355 m; lack of housing).
Concluding sentence: restate the main idea or give advice (Topic 1) or sum up the comparison (Topic 2).
Spend the last 5–10 minutes checking grammar (tenses, subject–verb agreement, articles), spelling, capital letters and punctuation. Keep to ONE paragraph of about 200 words.
marking_points: Content (8): relevant topic sentence and 3–4 developed supporting points; Topic 2 uses the table data and makes comparisons (both similarities and differences).
Organization (6): topic sentence, logically ordered supporting sentences with transitions, a concluding sentence; ONE paragraph; unity (no irrelevant sentences).
Language (6): grammar (tenses, agreement, articles, comparatives), vocabulary, spelling and punctuation.
Length: about 200 words; clearly shorter paragraphs lose content marks.

descriptors: 7–8: clear topic sentence; 3–4 well-developed, relevant supporting points with examples or explanations (Topic 2: uses most of the table and makes real comparisons – similarities AND differences); about 200 words.
5–6: relevant with some support, but one point is thin or repeated; some table data only listed, not compared.
3–4: few ideas, little support, partly off topic, or clearly too short (under about 120 words).
5–6: topic sentence → ordered supporting sentences → concluding sentence; one main idea only; smooth transitions (first of all, moreover, however, whereas, in conclusion).
3–4: logical overall, but weak or missing concluding sentence, few or repeated linkers, or one sentence off the main idea.
1–2: ideas in random order; no clear topic sentence; written as a list or several paragraphs.
5–6: accurate tenses, agreement and articles; varied sentence types; suitable vocabulary (comparatives/contrast words for Topic 2); correct spelling, capitals and punctuation.
3–4: several errors that do not block meaning; limited sentence variety or vocabulary.
1–2: frequent errors that sometimes block meaning.
0: errors make the paragraph impossible to follow.

Check (5 minutes): one paragraph, indent the first line; tenses, subject–verb agreement, articles, spelling, capitals, full stops; about 200 words.

Examiners check unity: every sentence must support the topic sentence. Delete sentences that drift away (e.g. the benefits of friends in Topic 1).
For comparison, use comparatives correctly: higher than, larger than, older than, more diverse than – never ‘more older’.

similar_questions.answer: Model: School A and School B are both secondary schools, but they differ in several important ways. First, School A is in the town centre, whereas School B is in a village 20 kilometres away. School A is also much bigger: it has 1,200 students, three times as many as School B, which has only 400. In addition, School A is older, having been founded in 1965, while School B opened in 2005. Their libraries show this difference: School A has a large library with old books, but School B has a small library with new computers. Each school has its own advantages. School A has experienced teachers, whereas School B offers a quiet environment for study. On the other hand, School A suffers from crowded classrooms, and many students at School B must walk a long way every day. In conclusion, School A is larger and more experienced, while School B is newer, smaller and quieter.

similar_questions.stem: Write a paragraph of about 200 words on the topic: ‘The advantages of having good friends’.
similar_questions.answer: Model: Good friends bring many advantages to a young person’s life. First of all, they give emotional support. When we fail an exam or lose a family member, a good friend listens to us and encourages us to keep going. Secondly, good friends help us in our studies. They share notes, explain difficult lessons and study with us before exams, so our results improve. In addition, good friends protect us from bad habits. Because they care about us, they warn us when we are making a mistake and set a good example by working hard and respecting others. Moreover, friendship makes life more enjoyable, since we can share our free time, hobbies and ideas with people we trust. Finally, good friends help us to become better people, because they tell us the truth about our weaknesses. In conclusion, good friends are a real treasure, so we should choose them carefully and be good friends to them in return.
